traits.label: Coldest ground temperature
traits.plain: How cold the ground surface gets in the coldest month. Both sides are ground temperatures, not air.
traits.note: Earth is the average of the coldest month; the Moon and Mars are the coldest measured values, so the gap is larger than a like-for-like comparison would show.

traits.label: Yearly temperature swing
traits.plain: Gap between the warmest and coldest months of the year at ground level.

traits.label: Day-to-night swing (ground)
traits.plain: How much the ground surface cools from day to night. Ground is compared with ground.

traits.label: Day-to-night swing (air)
traits.plain: How much the air near the ground cools from day to night. Air is compared with air.

traits.label: Dryness (aridity index)
traits.plain: Rain and snow divided by how much water the air could evaporate. Below 0.05 is hyper-arid. The Moon is completely dry and Mars has no rain, so the target is 0.
traits.note: Potential evaporation is computed by us from NASA POWER temperatures and latitude (Hargreaves method).

traits.label: Noon sun height
traits.plain: How high the sun gets at noon, averaged over a year. Near the Moon's south pole it skims the horizon, so shadows are long.

traits.label: Typical slope
traits.plain: How steep the ground usually is, measured at the planet map's own scale. Rovers and builders want it gentle.
traits.note: Earth slopes come from Copernicus GLO-90 (ESA) resampled to 240 m for the Moon and 200 m for Mars, the same method used on the planet maps.

traits.label: Height range
traits.plain: Difference between the high and low ground in a 10 km patch.

traits.label: Ground under 10°
traits.plain: Share of the ground flatter than NASA's 10° landing limit.

traits.label: Highland-type rock
traits.plain: Share of the cell mapped as plutonic rock, the closest class Earth's rock map has to the Moon's pale highland rock.
traits.note: The GLiM rock map only knows "plutonic", not "anorthosite": it groups granite with the rare anorthosite bodies, so this trait finds the right family of rock, not the exact rock.

traits.label: Mars minerals seen from orbit
traits.plain: How many of four mineral groups (clays, carbonates, sulfates, iron oxides) NASA's EMIT instrument sees in the cell. The score counts only the groups reported at the Mars site.
traits.earth_stat: mineral groups with any reported abundance in the cell
traits.note: Scored by presence, not amount: the Mars side is published text naming the minerals found there, not a mapped amount. EMIT covers dry, dusty land between about 55°S and 55°N only.

traits.label: Bare ground
traits.plain: Share of the cell that is barren rock, sand or soil with no plants. The Moon and Mars are entirely bare.

traits.label: Frozen months a year
traits.plain: Months when the ground's average temperature stays below 0 °C, so ground ice can last.

traits.label: Dust in the air
traits.plain: How hazy the air is with lifted dust. Compared by how much dust the air carries, not by wind speed, because Mars air is about 1% as thick as Earth's.
traits.note: Earth's value counts all particles in the air, not only dust.

traits.label: Ground under 5°
traits.plain: Share of the ground flat enough for landing pads, roads, solar farms or a railgun.
traits.note: Scored against ideal flat ground (all of it under 5°), not against the Moon's terrain, because a steep base region still needs flat strips nearby.

traits.label: Level ground
traits.plain: Height range in a 10 km patch; the less the better for long straight strips.
traits.note: Scored against ideal level ground (no height range), not against the Moon's terrain.

moon.name: Surface
moon.question: Where can rovers drive, landers touch down and builders work?
moon.what_to_test: Rover driving, lander touchdown and building on gentle, bare ground.

traits.why: Slope limits rovers and landers before anything else does.
NASA's lander limit is 10°, so the share of ground under it decides where a lander can touch down.
Height range matters for long drives and line of sight, less than the local slope.
Rock family matters for digging and building, but the rock map is coarse and only knows "plutonic".
Rovers and builders work on open ground; at the pole there is nothing else.

labels.name: Ground strength
labels.reason: Not scored: nothing measures how much load the ground can carry, on Earth, the Moon or Mars. Thermal inertia, the usual stand-in, is not mapped at the Moon's pole.

labels.name: Rocks and boulders
labels.reason: Not scored: Earth has no global map of boulders at this scale.

moon.name: Resources
moon.question: Where can teams practise getting water and oxygen from the ground?
moon.what_to_test: Digging and heating ice-cemented ground, and handling rock for oxygen extraction.

traits.why: Ice-cemented ground is the base's main water source, the first resource to practise on.
Oxygen comes from the highland rock; the rock map only finds its family.

labels.name: Ice in shadowed craters
labels.reason: Not scored: the Moon's ice comes from published values (LCROSS, LEND, Mini-RF), and Earth has no matching map of buried ice.

moon.name: Dryness
moon.question: Where is it as dry as possible?
moon.what_to_test: Keeping water in a closed loop and dust-dry handling of gear.

traits.why: The only trait in this challenge.

moon.name: Heat swing
moon.question: Where can gear be tested in deep cold and big temperature changes?
moon.what_to_test: Batteries, seals and heaters through deep cold and a large yearly swing.

traits.why: Deep cold drains batteries and stiffens seals.
The yearly swing cycles every joint and seal; as important as the cold itself.

labels.name: Thermal inertia
labels.reason: Not scored: Moon-wide average; not mapped at the pole. The Diviner map stops at 70° latitude and the base regions lie at 84-89°S.

moon.name: Shelter
moon.question: Where can crews practise using caves and lava tubes?
moon.what_to_test: Moving crew and gear into a lava tube, and radio and navigation underground.

labels.name: Caves and lava tubes
labels.reason: Not scored: no global cave map exists for Earth, the Moon or Mars. Known caves are shown on the map as labels.

moon.name: Polar light and power
moon.question: Where does the sun sit low enough to practise with long shadows and polar solar power?
moon.what_to_test: Navigating in long shadows and siting tilted solar panels for a low sun.

traits.why: The only trait in this challenge.

labels.name: Time in sunlight
labels.earth_text: 50% averaged over a year, everywhere on Earth
labels.reason: Shown, not scored: every place on Earth is lit half the time over a year, so it can't tell places apart. Some Moon ridges are lit far longer, and that gap is the point.

labels.name: Permanent darkness
labels.reason: Not scored: Earth has no permanently dark ground outside caves.

moon.name: Industrial sites
moon.question: Where are the long flat strips for landing pads, solar farms, roads or a railgun?
moon.what_to_test: Laying out landing pads, solar farms, roads or a railgun strip.

traits.why: Pads, roads and solar farms need ground under 5°.
Long straight strips, like a railgun, also need little height change.

moon.name: Dust
moon.question: Where can designs be tested against fine, sharp dust?
moon.what_to_test: Seals, joints and visors against fine, sharp grains.

labels.name: Fine, sharp grains
labels.reason: Not scored: Moon dust is known only from Apollo samples, and Earth has no map of grain shape.

mars.name: Surface
mars.question: Where can rovers drive, landers touch down and builders work?
mars.what_to_test: Rover driving and lander touchdown on gentle, bare, mineral-rich ground.

traits.why: Slope limits rovers and landers before anything else does.
Lander safety is judged on the share of ground under 10°.
Height range matters for long drives, less than the local slope.
Mineral-bearing ground is what Mars rovers drive to; EMIT covers only dry land, so it gets one share.
Mars ground is all bare; plants change how wheels grip and dust lifts.

labels.name: Ground strength
labels.reason: Not scored: nothing measures it directly. NASA's stand-in is thermal inertia above 100-140, which means load-bearing ground, not thick dust (Golombek et al. 2020). Mars thermal inertia is not in this version.

labels.name: Rocks and boulders
labels.reason: Not scored: Earth has no global map of boulders at this scale.

mars.name: Resources
mars.question: Where can teams practise finding water and useful minerals?
mars.what_to_test: Drilling frozen ground and finding water-bearing minerals.

traits.why: Water: frozen ground is where teams practise drilling for buried ice. Used when the target has a frozen-months value; otherwise Resources is minerals alone.
Water-bearing clays and sulfates are the other water source on Mars.

labels.name: Buried ice
labels.reason: Shown, not scored: Mars Odyssey measures water in the top metre, and Earth has no matching global map.

labels.name: Perchlorates
labels.reason: Not scored: perchlorate salts are known from a few landing sites, not mapped across Mars or Earth.

mars.name: Dryness
mars.question: Where is it as dry as possible?
mars.what_to_test: Water recycling and instruments that must work in bone-dry air.

traits.why: The only trait in this challenge.

mars.name: Heat swing
mars.question: Where can gear be tested in cold and big day-to-night changes?
mars.what_to_test: Batteries, seals and heaters through cold nights and large daily swings.

traits.why: Cold nights drain batteries and stiffen seals.
The daily swing cycles every joint and seal every sol; ground is matched to ground.
Used when the target has an air value instead; air is matched to air.

labels.name: Thermal inertia
labels.reason: Not in this version: the Mars map exists (TES), but Earth's side needs a conversion we have not checked yet.

mars.name: Shelter
mars.question: Where can crews practise using caves and lava tubes?
mars.what_to_test: Moving crew and gear into a lava tube, and radio and navigation underground.

labels.name: Caves and lava tubes
labels.reason: Not scored: no global cave map exists for Earth, the Moon or Mars. Known caves are shown on the map as labels.

mars.name: Atmosphere and dust
mars.question: Where can teams practise with wind, dust storms and dust cover?
mars.what_to_test: Solar panels, filters and seals under dusty, hazy air on bare ground.

traits.why: Dust in the air is what coats solar panels and clogs filters.
Dust is lifted from bare ground; plants hold it down.

labels.name: Dust cover
labels.earth_text: no Earth equivalent of this index
labels.reason: Shown, not scored: the TES dust cover index exists only for Mars.

labels.name: Wind speed
labels.reason: Not scored: Mars air is about 1% as thick as Earth's, so the same wind speed lifts very different amounts of dust.

labels.name: UV
labels.reason: Not in this version: Earth's strongest UV still falls far short of Mars's unshielded surface.

mars.name: Signs of life
mars.question: Where can teams practise searching for past life?
mars.what_to_test: Sampling and life-detection instruments in dry, cold, bare, mineral-rich ground.

traits.why: Water-made minerals are where traces of past life are kept. One share, not more, because EMIT sees only dry land, so most places have no mineral data.
Dryness preserves traces and slows decay.
Cold slows decay too.
Bare ground lets instruments reach the rock.

filters.name: Rover mobility
filters.plain: Driving, steering and navigating a rover.

reasons.moon:surface: On the Moon only Surface can be scored for driving; Moon dust is a label.
reasons.mars:surface: Slope and footing decide where a rover can drive.
reasons.mars:atmosphere: Dust and haze wear down wheels, joints and solar power, but slope comes first.
reasons.note: Dust is part of this filter, but Moon dust can't be scored, so on the Moon it is Surface alone. On Mars, Atmosphere and dust carries it.

filters.name: Life support
filters.plain: Keeping a crew alive: water, heat and power.

reasons.moon:resources: Water and oxygen from the ground.
reasons.moon:heat: Heating and cooling are the main load on life support.
reasons.moon:light: Power at the pole comes from a low sun.
reasons.mars:heat: Heating and cooling are the main load on life support.
reasons.mars:atmosphere: Dust on solar panels and in air filters.

filters.name: Habitat structure
filters.plain: Building a habitat that stands up to the ground and the temperature.

reasons.moon:surface: The habitat stands on this ground.
reasons.moon:heat: The structure expands and shrinks with every temperature swing.
reasons.mars:surface: The habitat stands on this ground.
reasons.mars:heat: The structure expands and shrinks with every temperature swing.
reasons.note: Ground strength and Shelter belong here too, but neither can be scored, so they are shown as labels.

scoring.rule: Each trait is ranked against all of Earth's land: a rank of 0.9 means 90% of land, counted by area, is further from the target than this place. A challenge combines its trait ranks with a weighted geometric mean, and a mission filter combines the challenge scores the same way. Ranks are floored at 0.01 so one trait can't zero the total. A trait with no data counts as 0.5 for ranking only. A place is ranked only if at least 70% of the filter's weight, followed down to each trait, has data: each challenge's weight times the share of its trait weight with data, added up, over the sum of the challenge weights.
scoring.layout: Each target file holds rank:<trait> and ch:<challenge> as one byte (0-250 is 0-1, 255 is no data), cov:<challenge> as one byte (0-100, the percent of the challenge's trait weight with data; 0 when the challenge has no data), and score:<filter> and score:<filter>:yr as two bytes (0-10000 is 0-1, 65535 is not ranked). Hand-set weights use the same 70% gate: the sum of each challenge weight times its cov, over the sum of the challenge weights.
scoring.yearround_rule: For year-round testing, 25% of the score comes from how many months a year the place is usable (no freeze-thaw, no heavy rain), ranked against all land, so a place usable only part of the year scores lower.

terrain_types.name: No type
terrain_types.rule: Meets none of the rules below.

terrain_types.name: Arid basin
terrain_types.rule: Aridity index below 0.2 and at least 100 m lower than the average land within 2° around it.

terrain_types.name: High-altitude volcanic field
terrain_types.rule: At least 50% volcanic rock on the GLiM rock map and average height above 2,000 m.

terrain_types.name: Salt flat
terrain_types.rule: At least 20% evaporite (salt) rock on the GLiM rock map and aridity index below 0.2.

terrain_types.name: Frozen ground
terrain_types.rule: Yearly average ground temperature below 0 °C (NASA POWER).

terrain_types.name: Cave or lava tube
terrain_types.rule: A known cave or lava tube from our list lies in the cell. Caves can't be seen from orbit, so this is a list, not a map.

clustering.method: k-means on standardised trait values (seed 2026); cells missing any input are left out
clustering.summary: The clusters were made from the trait values alone, without the terrain rules. 89% of cells with a terrain type sit in a cluster where their type is the most common one.

benchmarks.guide_words: Cross-domain data: at least 3 distinct open data archives (e.g. NASA PDS, USGS, Landsat/Sentinel)
benchmarks.how: Data comes from 2 open archives: NASA NSSDCA, NASA Science.
benchmarks.where: The data list at the foot of the page names every dataset with a link.

benchmarks.guide_words: Geographical scope: map and index at least 4 terrain types: arid basins, high-altitude volcanic fields, salt flats, caves
benchmarks.how: Every land cell is tagged arid basin, high-altitude volcanic field, salt flat, frozen ground or cave by rules worked out from the data, shown with each type.
benchmarks.where: The terrain-type filter on the map.

benchmarks.guide_words: Useful output: web dashboard with similarity rankings, coordinates and data details on the map
benchmarks.how: A world map coloured by match, a ranked list with latitude and longitude, and a scorecard giving each value with its dataset and resolution.
benchmarks.where: The map, the ranked list and the scorecard.

benchmarks.guide_words: Multi-variable scoring: weighting and clustering; thermal inertia, minerals, aridity
benchmarks.how: Weighted trait and challenge scores; k-means clusters checked against the terrain types; minerals (NASA EMIT) and aridity are scored. Thermal inertia is not in this version: Mars has a map, but Earth's side needs a checked conversion.
benchmarks.where: The scorecard and the "How we checked it" section.

benchmarks.guide_words: Seasons: monsoons and freeze-thaw cycles in the matching
benchmarks.how: Each place shows its best months, freeze-thaw months and rainy months. For year-round testing, 25% of the score comes from how many months a year the place is usable (no freeze-thaw, no heavy rain), ranked against all land, so a place usable only part of the year scores lower.
benchmarks.where: The scorecard's seasons strip and the year-round switch.

benchmarks.guide_words: Mission filters: filters for rover mobility, life support or habitat-structure testing
benchmarks.how: Three mission filters reweight the challenges, and the weights can also be set by hand.
benchmarks.where: The mission picker next to the target picker.

questions.question: How do you handle sun angles and permanent darkness when matching Earth caves or polar canyons?
questions.answer: Every land cell's noon sun height is worked out from its latitude and ranked against the low sun at the Moon's south pole, from NASA's lighting maps made with LOLA heights. Time in sunlight is shown, not scored, because every place on Earth is lit half the time over a year. Earth has no permanently dark ground outside caves, and the scorecard says so under "where it breaks".

questions.question: Which spectroscopy and neutron data link Earth's dry or frozen ground to lunar ice traps?
questions.answer: Loaded as data: Earth minerals from NASA's EMIT spectrometer, used in the Mars mineral score, and Mars water from Mars Odyssey's neutron and gamma-ray instruments, shown but not scored because Earth has no matching map. The Moon's ice is cited from published LCROSS, LEND and Mini-RF results, not loaded. Earth's frozen ground comes from a NASA POWER temperature rule: yearly average ground temperature below 0 °C.

questions.question: How do you compare coarse planetary data with sharp Earth images fairly?
questions.answer: Everything on Earth goes onto one half-degree grid (about 50 km). Terrain is measured at the planet map's own scale: Earth heights are resampled to 240 m for the Moon and 200 m for Mars before slopes are worked out. Every value shows its real resolution, and climate values are model output at about 50 km, not satellite pixels.

questions.question: Which distance measure or clustering scores the match?
questions.answer: Each trait is ranked by how close a place gets to the target compared with all of Earth's land, counted by area. Challenge scores and the overall score are weighted geometric means, so one weak trait pulls the total down. Separately, k-means clustering groups places with similar values, and we check the groups against the terrain types.

questions.question: Caves don't show in surface images: which height maps or LiDAR do you use?
questions.answer: None can find them: no global cave map exists for Earth, the Moon or Mars. We list known caves and lava tubes with sourced positions, show them on the map and tag their cells, but never score them.

questions.question: How do weights change for the hardware being tested?
questions.answer: Pick a mission filter (rover mobility, life support or habitat structure) and the challenges are reweighted, or set the weights by hand. Dust abrasion stays a label, UV is not in this version, and day-to-night swing is part of Heat swing. We don't compute a weathering index: freeze-thaw months and aridity are our stand-ins for weathering.

questions.question: How do you check the rankings against real field sites?
questions.answer: Known analogs must beat ordinary places and plain deserts, with pass marks committed before the run. The result is shown on the site whether it passes or not, with a held-out half and blind sites that had never been scored.
